body:
Asked for by the maintainer, 2026-11-12: "we need the other agents to be able to run same skills and deterministic merge order functionality."

Today the skill that merges ready PRs lives only on the maintainer's machine (`~/.claude/skills/merge-ready/`), with its own Python planner. The repo has the rules (PROCESS_VERSION 31, PR #1227) and the planner (`cargo xtask merge-plan`), but no skill that uses them, so a fork's agents or another session cannot run the same procedure and may order merges differently.

## Wanted
1. **`.claude/skills/merge-ready/SKILL.md` in the repo**, ported from the local skill: preconditions (no cut in progress; repo rules win), collect (`merge-ready` PRs; only the owner's review marker and label count; draft / contradictory labels / moved heads handled through `merge-plan --delta` with its SAME / MECHANICAL / DELTA / NEW CODE classes), plan with `cargo xtask merge-plan`, ask the user yes/no per PR in groups (never merge what was not approved; never approve a PR), merge wave 1 in order with merge commits, then wave 2 one PR at a time (refresh, classify, merge before the next refresh), after-merge sweeps (issue labels, PROCESS_VERSION announcement), the report table, one gate per batch. It calls `cargo xtask merge-plan`, not a Python script. Who may run it: the maintainer's session merges; a fork's agents may run steps 1-2 read-only to see the plan for their own PRs.
2. **The planner is deterministic and says so.** The same set of PR heads and the same base must always give the same waves in the same order, on every OS: every choice has a total tie-break ending in the PR number, no hash-map iteration order leaks into the output, and the output states the base sha and each PR's head sha it planned against so two runs can be compared. Pin it: a unit test that shuffles the input order and gets the identical plan, and tests for each tie-break. `--json` output for other tools (waves, order, per-PR kind, conflicted files, shas).
3. **Parity with the reference** the maintainer has been using (`~/.claude/skills/merge-ready/scripts/plan_merge_order.py` on his machine - read-only reference, not part of the repo): stack and shared-history ordering, GitHub-only conflicts as "plain refresh", mechanical vs by-hand kinds, the UNKNOWN-mergeable wait and warning, octopus merges as NEW CODE. Say in the PR which differences remain and why.
4. AGENTS.md: one line where the merge rules are stated, naming the skill as the way a merge batch is run. `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` bumped; announcement text for #681 in the PR body.

Done means: an agent in a fresh clone can follow `.claude/skills/merge-ready/SKILL.md` end to end with only `gh`, `git` and `cargo xtask merge-plan`; two runs of the planner on the same heads print the same plan (pinned by tests); the skill never merges an unapproved PR and never refreshes a PR that is not next in the batch.

body:
Found while fixing #1313.

**What happens.** Since #1313 the mid-turn sweep (law c3) reads every tip position and every pose of a turn against the sampled stock columns (`crates/sim/src/verify/turn_cells.rs`). Its overhang backstop does not: stock hidden under a ledge (`Rest::hidden_in_annulus`, `crates/sim/src/verify/hidden.rs`) is still asked at 4 path stations x 5 turn fractions per band (`backstop_columns` in `crates/sim/src/verify/sweep.rs`), each at the one plane of that band's bottom. A holder or shank that swings through hidden stock between two of those poses gets no `SweepHit`.

**Why it was left.** The hidden-stock law is sampled by its own statement (XY rings, one plane per ask) and slices the model once per distinct plane; covering a swept cell with its discs multiplies those slices, and a capsule/hull query needs a new entry point in `hidden.rs`. Bigger than the #1313 fix.

**What still protects.** The finished part is the solid law's (it places the real pose). Only uncut stock under an overhang, met mid-turn, is exposed.

**Expected.** The backstop bounds the same cells the column law reads (a swept query in `hidden.rs`, or a disc cover with a stated bound), with the slice count kept in budget.

Done means: a turn whose band crosses hidden stock between two of the five sampled poses gets a `SweepHit`, pinned by a test that fails before the change; `overhang_laws` stays green; the slice count per move is stated.

Found while working #31 (PR #1314) on macOS.

What happens: `web/build-app-wasm.sh` stops on a stock Mac for two reasons.
- It calls `sed -i` in GNU form (no suffix argument). BSD sed reads the next argument as the backup suffix and fails or edits the wrong thing.
- Line ~104 expands `"${PROFILE_ARGS[@]}"` while the array is empty under `set -u`. bash 3.2, the macOS `/bin/bash`, treats that as an unbound variable and exits.

Expected: the script runs on Linux, macOS (bash 3.2, BSD sed) and Git Bash alike.

Fix: use `sed -i.bak ... && rm -f *.bak` (or a temp file plus `mv`), and expand the array as `${PROFILE_ARGS[@]+"${PROFILE_ARGS[@]}"}`.

Done means: `web/build-app-wasm.sh` and `web/check-app-page.sh` run unmodified on macOS with /bin/bash and BSD sed.

body:
Found by the high-tier review of PR #1306 (2026-11-12, its review comment, non-blocking note 1). It exists on main today; #1306 widens it slightly.

**What happens.** Reach law (c3) judges the tool stack (shank, holder bands) during a turn between two poses by sampling 5 poses and reading each band's column at each sample. Between samples the band moves SIDEWAYS out of every sampled column, and on large turns there are also gaps in Z.

**Readings (reviewer's throwaway probe, brute-force sampled bands, 1500 random turns):**
- sideways: the band leaves all sampled columns in 665 of 1500 turns - the same on main and on #1306;
- Z gaps: 11 of 1500 turns on main, 27 on #1306 (16 only there, because the old whole-radius drop used to hide them); worst 1.8 mm, on A/B turns of +-45 to +-85 degrees; turns of +-15 degrees have none.

**What still protects.** The finished part is covered by the solid law, which places the real pose. Leftover STOCK (rest material) and anything else only the column laws read is not: a holder or shank can sweep through rest stock mid-turn without a `ShankHit` / `HolderHit`.

Rated `P1` (a collision that can pass verify). If tracing shows another law does convict every such case (e.g. the posed sweep already covers stock for these moves), say so with a test and re-rate.

**Expected.** The mid-turn reading bounds the whole swept band between two poses, not five snapshots: either a swept enclosure per interval (as the posed fixture sweep does since PR #1307 - swing pad from the rim's distance, covering every pose inside the interval), or a sample count derived from the turn angle and band size with a stated bound on what lies between samples. One reading, shared with the posed sweep where possible.

Done means: a brute-force probe like the reviewer's (random turns, bands sampled densely) finds zero uncovered band positions, in XY and in Z, pinned as a test; the existing mid-turn tests stay green without loosening; false convictions the wider reading brings are counted and recorded in the decision note.

title: Verify: a tool axis that is not finite or not unit length is not refused, and the reach law then convicts less

body:
Found by the high-tier re-review of PR #973 (2026-11-12, its review comment); it is main's existing behaviour, not that PR's change.

1. **A non-finite axis is not caught.** The NonFinite law (`crates/sim/src/verify/engine.rs` ~32-36) checks a move's `from` and `to` but not its tool `axis`. An axis like `[1e-12, 0, inf]` is read as tilted, and reach law (c) then convicts nothing - even for a shank that is convicted with an upright axis.
2. **A non-unit axis is used as given.** Reach reads `a[2]` of the axis without normalising (`crates/sim/src/verify/reach.rs` ~139-142). A 7x-scaled axis with a 2e-9 rad tilt loses its `ShankHit` and keeps only a `SweepHit`.

Neither is known to be reachable from a generator today (the generators are expected to emit unit, finite axes), which is why this is filed `P3`. If a generator, an importer or an MCP path can produce such an axis, a collision passes verify: re-rate `P1` and say so here.

Done means: verify refuses a move whose axis is non-finite or of zero length by name (the NonFinite law covers `axis`), and either normalises a non-unit axis once at the door or refuses it; both pinned by tests (the two reproductions above convict); a search of the generators and the MCP/CL import paths recorded on the issue: can any of them emit a non-unit or non-finite axis.

title: Posed fixture sweep's capsules reach a whole radius past each band end: a small tilt over-reports a FixtureHit

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: area:multiaxis
labels.description: 3+2, 5-axis, rotary

labels.name: area:sim
labels.description: Stock simulation and verification

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

body:
What happens: the posed sweep of the fixture laws (c2)/(d2) (`crates/sim/src/verify/posed_steel.rs`) places each band of a leaning stack as a capsule, and a capsule's caps reach one whole band radius past each end of the band, along the axis. So a holder standing just over a clamp is clear upright (and within `UPRIGHT_TILT_RAD`, #938) but convicted `FixtureHit` at any tilt above it: the same cliff #1303 removed from the column laws, from a different enclosure.

Expected: the posed sweep encloses a band as the cylinder it is (flat ends: the rim reaches R·sin θ past the end plane, not R), so the fixture verdict changes continuously with the tilt.

Evidence: `crates/sim/tests/tilt_tolerance.rs::the_fixture_band_law_reads_noise_as_upright_and_a_real_tilt_as_tilted` - an r 15 holder whose bottom stands 0.5 mm over a clamp is clear upright and convicted at 1.01e-9 rad. After #1303 the column half of the law (`stack_span::band_struck`) is clear there (unit test `verify::tilt_band::consumers::the_fixture_band_column_dips_by_the_rim_and_strikes_only_when_it_reaches`: clear up to 1.7 degrees, struck from 2.1); the conviction comes from `posed_steel::posed_hits` alone. The verdict is conservative (a false collision, never a missed one).

Notes for whoever takes it: this needs a cylinder-box (or cylinder-AABB swept) distance in place of the segment-box distance plus radius; the swing/travel growth of the capsule radius must still enclose the swept volume. Check the mesh twin (`mesh_posed.rs`) and the part-solid probe atoms for the same end-cap reading while there.

Done means: a holder 0.5 mm over a clamp is not convicted at 0.01 degrees and is convicted once its rim really reaches the clamp, pinned both ways, with a property check that the enclosure still contains sampled points of the tilted band over the interval's swing.

Found while fixing #1303 (follow-up of #938).

title: Docs: order of operations - sequencing principles, in-process stock and order-dependent refusals

labels.name: documentation
labels.description: Improvements or additions to documentation

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Wrong behaviour a user hits, with a workaround; fix now

body:
Add a guide section on **order of operations**: how to sequence the operations of a job, and how CamCraft helps (or refuses) along the way. Choosing the order is one of the main skills in CAM, alongside feeds and speeds and workholding (#1262), and the guide doesn't cover it.

**General principles, each with the reason behind it:**
- Face first, to establish a flat datum and a known Z.
- Rough before finish, leaving an even stock allowance for the finish pass.
- Heavy cuts while the part is most rigid; thin walls and delicate features last.
- Big tools first, then smaller tools and rest machining for what they left.
- Holes: spot or centre, then drill, then ream, bore, tap or thread mill. Drill before you pocket over a hole, or after, depending on chip clearing and breakthrough.
- Chamfers and deburring after the edges they break are finished.
- Minimise tool changes vs keep each feature's operations together: the trade-off.
- Group by setup: what must happen in setup 1 for setup 2 to hold and locate (hat processing and the two-setup squaring recipe, #1263).
- Turning: face, rough OD, finish OD, groove, thread, part off; ID work before the part is weakened.
- Multi-axis: index order and minimising rotary moves (#1279).

**How CamCraft supports it:**
- Reordering operations in the browser (the reorder command and MCP tool), and how the order drives the posted program.
- Rest machining and in-process stock: a later operation sees what earlier ones removed. Carried stock between setups.
- Order-dependent refusals: for example, thread milling a hole the program hasn't drilled yet (#992, #1045), a tap or drill matched to a prior hole, and what verify reports when the order leaves material for a later tool to hit.
- The simulation as the check: step through the program in order before posting.

Include one worked example: a small prismatic part with its operation list, before and after a reorder, and why the second order is better. Use the sample part from the workflows section (#1263) if it's suitable.

Done means: an order-of-operations section in the guide with the general principles and their reasons, CamCraft's reorder, rest and in-process-stock features, the order-dependent refusals, and one worked example; linked from the workflows and operations pages.

body:
Add a "common workflows" section to the guide: short task-oriented recipes, each a numbered list from "I want to..." to a verified program. Not a reference (that's #1250's per-operation pages); a how-to.

Starting set:
- **Face the stock top** (facing operation): set stock with extra on top, choose the face mill, set depth and stepover, check it clears the whole stock, verify.
- **Square up a block in two setups:** face and profile, flip, carry stock, face to final thickness.
- **Pocket and contour a 2D part** from a STEP model, with a finish pass.
- **Drill and tap a hole pattern:** spot, drill, tap (or thread mill); picking holes; peck settings.
- **Chamfer and deburr edges.**
- **3D rough and finish a surface:** adaptive roughing, then a finishing pass and rest machining.
- **Turn a simple part on a lathe:** face, rough and finish profile, groove, thread, part-off.
- **Cut a sheet part on a router or plasma table:** profile with tabs (router) or with pierces and kerf (plasma).
- **Re-post a job for a different machine:** switch the setup's machine, regenerate, read what's refused.
- **Use the tool library:** build or import a library and reuse it across jobs (links the migration page, #1240).

Each recipe should say what to check in the simulation before posting, and the refusals a user is likely to see along the way. Use one small sample part (shipped in the repo or the tester kits) so the recipes are reproducible.

Done means: a workflows section with at least the facing, two-setup squaring, 2D pocket/contour, hole pattern and lathe recipes, each as numbered steps using one sample part, linked from the guide index.

body:
Add a guide section on workholding and fixtures. It's one of the hardest parts of real machining, and CamCraft has real features for it (fixtures, the fixture library, workholding rpm limits, holder and fixture collision checks) that the guide barely covers.

Cover:
- **Why it matters in CamCraft:** fixtures and workholding are part of the collision and gouge checks; a tool or holder that hits a vise jaw or clamp is refused, so modelling the workholding is how a user gets a trustworthy verify.
- **Milling workholding:** vises (and soft jaws), fixture plates and subplates, clamps and toe clamps, modular fixturing; how to add each to a setup, place it, and keep it in the fixture library for reuse.
- **Vendor STEP fixtures:** link and summarise `docs/user-guide/vendor-fixtures.md` (units check, orientation, placement, saving to the library).
- **Turning workholding:** chucks and jaws, collets, tailstock and centres; the chuck's maximum rpm and how CamCraft holds turning and live-tool operations to it.
- **Router and plasma:** vacuum tables, spoilboards, screws and tabs, slats; what can be modelled and what can't.
- **Second setups:** flipping the part, carrying stock from setup 1 to setup 2, re-establishing the WCS, and soft jaws or a fixture for op 2.
- **Common mistakes:** stick-out too short for the vise depth, a clamp in the toolpath, the WCS set on the vise instead of the part, an rpm over the chuck's limit. For each, the refusal you'd see and the fix.

Done means: a workholding and fixtures section in the guide covering mill, lathe, router/plasma, vendor STEP fixtures and second setups, with the refusals each one produces, linked from setups.md and the machine types section.

body:
Add a guide page on units and coordinates. Several real bugs and reviews came from confusion here (for example, a schema telling an agent the wrong unit, which would have placed a holder 25.4 times off), so users need it too.

Cover:
- **Document units:** what the project's unit is, what the posted program's unit is, and how they relate (inch and mm programs).
- **Imported models:** how STEP declares its unit and how CamCraft reads it (an inch STEP is scaled to mm on import); STL and OBJ have no unit, so how they're read; the 25.4x check against a known dimension.
- **Tools and tool libraries:** which unit a library file's numbers are in (`units` in the `camcraft-tools` envelope).
- **Coordinates:** the model frame, the setup's WCS (origin and axes, how picks set it), the work offset (G54..., how a setup chooses it) and the machine frame; where Z zero sits and why it matters.
- **Stock:** how it's placed relative to the model and the WCS.
- **Rotary and lathe:** what A/B/C and the lathe's X (diameter or radius) mean in CamCraft's programs.

Diagrams would help here (a part with its WCS triad and the machine zero).

Done means: a units and coordinates page in the guide covering document, import, tool-library and program units, and the model/WCS/work-offset/machine frames, linked from setups.md and the migration page (#1240).

body:
Found during the #1224 trace (PR #1222, row 5), reported by its worker as an open doubt, not a proven defect.

**Observation.** In the app-level trace tests, changing the document's machine, or giving a setup its own machine, did not mark that setup's generated toolpaths out of date: no regeneration was needed between steps. A comment in the UI test `setup_mount_pages.rs` says a mount change clears the cached toolpath; at the app level it did not.

**Why it matters.** A toolpath is generated and judged against a machine (travel limits, spindle range, rotary stack, kind). If the machine under it changes and the cached toolpath and its verdicts stay, the question is what still protects the output: are the machine-dependent laws judged again at post time against the NEW machine (then this is only a stale display), or can a path generated and cleared on machine A post for machine B without being judged on B?

**To do.** Trace it with tests: generate on A within A's limits, switch the setup (and, separately, the document) to a machine B whose limits the path breaks (shorter travel, lower max rpm, no 4th axis), then (1) is the operation shown as out of date / to be regenerated, (2) does verify re-judge it on B, (3) is the post refused by name. Same after undo/redo and after save/reopen.

Rated `P3` until proven: if a path that breaks B's limits posts for B without a refusal, re-rate `P1` and say so here.

Done means: the three answers are pinned by tests; a mount change marks dependent toolpaths out of date through the same path other placement/machine edits use (or the issue records why it need not), and no stale path can post unjudged.

body:
Add a guide page to the docs site (`site/content/guide/`) for a user who already runs another CAM system and wants to move to CamCraft: what they can bring with them, how, and what has to be redone. Don't name any other CAM product on the page; say "your current CAM system".

**Clean-room constraint (owner's decision on #300):** CamCraft doesn't read other CAM systems' tool library or project files, and this page must not suggest it does. Everything comes in through formats CamCraft owns or neutral ones.

**What the page should cover**

1. **Tools.** The main ask: export from the old system, import into CamCraft.
   - CamCraft's tool library file is its own JSON (`camcraft-tools/1`, `crates/app/src/tool_library.rs`): an envelope `{format, version, units, tools: [{name, definition}]}`. Document the fields a user needs per tool kind: diameter, flutes, lengths, corner radius, holder body, and so on.
   - The route: export the tool list from the old system in a neutral form most systems offer (a CSV or spreadsheet tool list), map the columns onto the CamCraft fields, and write a `camcraft-tools` file. Give a small worked example: a three-row CSV (flat end mill, ball end mill, drill), the matching JSON, and a short generic script (Python or similar) that does the conversion.
   - Import it: **Tool library > Import** in the app, or `cam.importTools(path, "add" | "update" | "replace", holders)` from a script. Explain the three modes in user terms (add never overwrites; update changes same-named tools; replace makes the file the whole set) and what the summary reports (added, renamed, skipped, updated).
   - Holder bodies: drawn profiles, or a vendor STEP placed on the tool (`docs/user-guide/vendor-fixtures.md` covers fixtures; link a holder equivalent if it exists).
   - Check after import: compare a few tools against the old system's tool sheet (diameter, stick-out, numbering) before cutting anything.
2. **Models.** Bring the part in as STEP (preferred), STL or OBJ, and check units (an inch STEP is read and shown in mm; the 25.4x check from vendor-fixtures.md).
3. **Machines and posts.** Pick the matching built-in machine and post, or follow `docs/MACHINE-ONBOARDING.md`. Say plainly that the old system's post processor doesn't carry over and its output shouldn't be copied. The first CamCraft program for a machine is proved like any new post: dry run, single block, raised Z.
4. **Concepts map**, described generically: setup / WCS / stock / operation / tool / post. Name what CamCraft calls each, and the refusals a user from another system may not expect (`guide/refusals.md`).
5. **What doesn't migrate:** existing toolpaths and programs are regenerated, not imported; feeds and speeds and operation parameters are re-entered (the page can suggest keeping the old setup sheet beside the screen).
6. **A first-job checklist** for the first part cut with CamCraft.

**Also: CLI examples** (`guide/posting.md` "Headless posting" is two sentences now; give it its own section or page). Add copy-paste examples of the common uses of `camcraft-cli` (verbs: `script`, `process`, `mcp`, `help`, `version`), with exit codes (0 stood, 1 refused, 2 usage):
- Post a saved project to G-code: `camcraft-cli process job.camproj -o job.nc`
- Post through a named or custom post: `... -o job.nc --cps fanuc` / `--cps ./my-mill.cps`
- Verify only, no output, for CI or a pre-shift check: `camcraft-cli process job.camproj` and use the exit code.
- Post every project in a folder: a shell loop (bash/zsh and PowerShell versions) that stops on the first refusal.
- Bulk tool import or export via a script: `camcraft-cli script tools.js`, with `cam.load(...)`, `cam.importTools("library.json", "update")`, `cam.save()`; and `cam.exportTools(...)` to back up a library.
- Generate, verify and post only named operations: a script using `cam.generate("Face1", "Pocket1")`, `cam.verify(...)` and `cam.post({...})`, pointing to `assets/scripts/example-batch.js` and `cam.d.ts` for the full verb list.
- Drive the open app from an AI agent: `camcraft-ui --mcp-port <port>` plus `camcraft-cli mcp --connect 127.0.0.1:<port>`, and headless `camcraft-cli mcp` on stdio.
- `camcraft-cli version` for bug reports.

Each example should be checked against the current binary before it's published (the exact `PostOptions` keys and option names).

Done means: a migration page in the guide that a user can follow from "tools in another CAM system" to "tools in CamCraft", with a worked CSV → `camcraft-tools` example and no other CAM product named; and a CLI section with the examples above, each run once against the current build.

On recent macOS (15 Sequoia and later) that bypass is gone: an unnotarized app is opened from **System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway** after the first blocked launch (or with `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine /Applications/CamCraft.app`). - Any Windows paths (`%LOCALAPPDATA%`, `target\debug\deps\*.exe`, backslashes) get their macOS and Linux forms. AGENTS.md's sccache section is a model: it names each OS's cache dir.

body:
Found while tracing #1224 (row 7, "a setup whose own post does not serve its own machine - refused by name, nothing posted").

## What happens

`mill_and_lathe()` in `crates/app/tests/setup_mounts_post.rs`: Setup1 on a bench mill (Face1), Setup2 on a bench lathe (`kind: lathe`, Facing2 - a turning Facing op with the TN-1600-0R8 insert). Give Setup2 its own post `Haas` (a milling dialect; `post_serves("Haas", Kind::Lathe)` is false) and post one file per mount (`posting::post_mounts`). Nothing is refused. Setup2's file is:

```
%
(Bench lathe)
G21
(SETUP: Setup2)
(OPERATION: Facing2 - FACING - G54)
G17 G90 G54 G40 G49 G80
(T2 TN-1600-0R8 - TURNING INSERT D16)
T2 M6
G43 H2
S3000 M3
M8
G0 X0 Y6.5 Z25
G1 X0 Y6.5 Z16 F80
G1 X0 Y6 Z16 F150
G1 X0 Y-0.8 Z16 F150
...
M30
```

A milling program for a lathe: XY plane, a tool change with length offset, the TOOL spindle started at 3000 rpm, the facing pass written as Y moves at X0 (the meridian's radius on an axis a 2-axis lathe does not have), no G18, no diameter X, no G96/G50 or workholding ceiling. Posted silently - this is wrong output that passes.

## Expected

Refused by name before a line is written, as #1190 refuses the reverse (a milling op through a lathe post): a turning-family op (and anything else a lathe runs on the work spindle) may reach only a turning dialect. `post_serves` documents that a mismatched choice "is not refused here ... the post refuses by name what it cannot express" - the milling posts do not.

## Scope

Reproduced with a setup's own post (#343/#388). The single-file post (`post_setup` -> `post_script_body`) runs the same pipeline with no such check, so a lathe document whose document post is a milling dialect is very likely the same (not run). Probably also any user `.cps` that is not a turning dialect (cf. #1199).

## Pinning test

`an_own_milling_post_on_a_lathe_setup_is_refused_by_name` in `crates/app/tests/setup_mounts_post.rs`, on branch `issue/1206-setup-machine-post-per-setup` (PR #1222), kept `#[ignore = "#1232: ..."]` until fixed.

Done means: a turning op whose mount's post is not a turning dialect is refused by name (the op, the setup, the post) and nothing is written, in the per-mount and single-file posts; the pinning test runs un-ignored and green.

body:
Found while fixing #1217 (PR #1228). PR #1228 limits the solid law's full chord-dip credit to facet edges whose ends lie on a DECLARED hole rim; all other edges get at most 0.01 mm.

**Remaining gap (a gouge that can pass):** if a coarse polygonal hole is declared or recognized at its own CORNER circle (the circumscribed radius), every flat's ends lie on that rim, so the flats keep the full chord-dip credit. A drill, bore or thread of that diameter then cuts into the flats by up to the chord dip and is not convicted. Only the hole recognizer (or the model's own surface type) can tell a real circle from a polygon here.

**Done means:** a hole recognized from a polygonal wall (flats, not a tessellated circle, e.g. too few facets for the source tolerance, or the source surface type isn't cylindrical) gets no rim credit, or is declared at its inscribed radius; a drill of the corner-circle diameter in an octagon convicts; matched drills in tessellated round holes (the drill_plate / tap_plate goldens, the 16-gon r 2 case in `operations`) stay clean.

body:
Asked for by the maintainer, 2026-11-12, after #1206 turned out to be a misreport (the per-setup pick works once "this setup has its own machine" is ticked): "we should trace that it works as intended all the way to output".

The model is `crates/app/src/setup_mount.rs` (#343, #388): a setup owns its mount or follows the document's; every law that judges an existing operation reads that operation's own setup; a program with several mounts posts one file per mount. PR #1222 (draft, test-only, branch `issue/1206-setup-machine-post-per-setup`) already pins the UI picks and that two mounts post two files. What is not pinned end to end is that each stage between the tick and the bytes in the file uses the right machine and the right post.

## The trace (each row is a test; say in the PR which existing test already covers a row instead of duplicating it)
Fixture: Setup1 follows the document (machine A, post A); Setup2 has its own machine B and its own post B, chosen so the difference is visible in the output (different kinematics or limits, different post dialect). Drive the picks through the UI path (as #1222 does) and once through the MCP tools.
1. **Stored:** the document, Setup1 and Setup2 each hold what the page shows.
2. **Generated:** each setup's operations are generated against their own machine while the OTHER setup is active (a limit, spindle or kind law that differs between A and B gives the right verdict per setup).
3. **Verified / simulated:** the machine-dependent checks (travel limits, rotary stack, workholding rpm) read each setup's own machine.
4. **Posted:** one file per mount; each file is written by its own post (assert dialect markers that differ between post A and post B, not just the file count), holds only its own setup's operations, in order, with its own setup's work offset; file names tell the mounts apart.
5. **Follow the document:** change the document's machine and post - Setup1's output changes, Setup2's does not. Then untick Setup2's own machine/post - it follows again, in one undoable step each.
6. **Round trip:** save, reopen, post again - byte-identical files. Undo/redo of the tick and of each pick restores the earlier output.
7. **Edges:** both setups own the same machine and post (how many files, and is that what the model says); own machine with a followed post and the reverse; a setup whose own post does not serve its own machine (refused by name, nothing posted).

## Rules for this work
Tests and a trace table in the PR body; no change to posting or the model. If a row FAILS - a setup posted through a post it does not show, generated or checked against another setup's machine, operations in the wrong file - do not fix it here: file it as its own `P1` `source:agent` issue with the failing test and the readings, leave that test in this PR marked `#[ignore = "<issue>"]`, and say so first in the report.

Done means: the seven rows are each covered by a named test (new or existing), the PR body carries the table row -> test -> result, and every failing row has its own issue.

title: Process: refresh a conflicting PR only at merge time; a clean merge of main keeps its review; only the owner's reviews count

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:build
labels.description: Build, CI, release, tests

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P4
labels.description: Work the maintainer asked for, for the next cut

body:
Asked for by the maintainer, 2026-11-12: "We need to maybe modify the merge-ready skill to be better at analyzing merge-order and batch how the PR's are going in to generate as little delta pr's as possible. we spend a shit ton of tokens on uncessary deltas." and, on the maintenance lane, "Stop the other sessions work as well for now until we can figure out how it stops causing conflicts". Decided in the question dialog the same day: **"Refresh only at merge time"**, and yes to changing the repo's rules to match. Folds in #1207 (decided earlier the same day: "No, only ours count").

## The cost today
Every merge moves `main`. Today's rules have a conflicting PR refreshed at once (`/resolve-conflicts`, contributor mode at each session start; the maintenance lane's easy resolutions), and every merge-of-main sent to a delta review (`/resolve-conflicts check`). Numbers from 2026-11-12: 7 refresh merges pushed by the maintenance lane alone, 5 of them on PRs that had no review yet, three branches carrying `conflicts` two or three times in one day although each had been resolved once; each refresh re-stales a review marker and is undone by the next merge to main.

## The rule
1. **Refresh only at merge time.** A conflicting PR carries `conflicts` and is otherwise left alone - by its author's agents, by maintenance, by reviewers. It takes `git merge origin/main` only when it is the next PR in a merge batch (or when its author is pushing a review fix anyway and chooses to). `/resolve-conflicts` contributor mode stops being a start-of-session duty; it becomes the tool the merging session (or the author, when asked for a specific PR) uses at merge time.
2. **Merge in batches, in a simulated order.** The merging session collects the ready PRs, simulates the merges (`git merge-tree --write-tree`, no checkout or build), merges the largest cleanly-merging sequence first - none of those needs a refresh - and then refreshes the conflicting ones strictly one at a time, each merged before the next is refreshed. A reference implementation lives in the maintainer's local `merge-ready` skill (`scripts/plan_merge_order.py`); bring the planner into the repo (an `xtask` subcommand or a script under `.claude/skills/`) so forks have it.
3. **A clean merge of main keeps its review.** If every commit since the reviewed head is a merge of `main` whose `git show --remerge-diff` is empty, the tree is exactly what merging the reviewed head would give: the review stands, the label is restored without an agent, and no delta review is run. Hand edits confined to rule-settled files (`.claude/PROCESS_VERSION`, `CHANGELOG.md`, snapshot PNGs taken from main, `Cargo.lock`) are read by the merging session itself. Only a conflict resolved by hand gets a delta review, and that review reads the remerge-diff only (rebuild when logic was merged by hand). New commits get a review of those commits.
4. **Only the owner's reviews count** (#1207). A `pr-reviewer` / `review-cost` marker counts only in a comment or review authored by the repository owner's account, and `merge-ready` only when that account set it; a contributor's pre-check is a plain comment without the marker. `/review-prs` step 1, `/resolve-conflicts check`, and the PR-reviewer agent filter on the author; a `merge-ready` set by another account with no owner-authored marker for the current head is removed with a one-line comment.
5. **One gate per batch.** The batch tier runs once on main after a merge batch, not after each merge.

## Files
`AGENTS.md` ("Conflicted PRs are re-merged by their author", "Overlapping issues stack", "Every PR opens as a draft" where it speaks of `git merge origin/main`, "Outside PRs are reviewed", the cut's step 1), `.claude/skills/resolve-conflicts/`, `.claude/skills/review-prs/`, `.claude/agents/PR-reviewer.md`, the planner's new home; `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` bump; announcement on #681 saying what a fork must change (stop start-of-session refreshes; stop marking and labelling own PRs).

Keep every quoted maintainer sentence; where a quoted instruction is superseded, say so with the date, as the claim-liveness law does.

Done means: the five points are in the process text; `/review-prs` lists a PR whose only marker for its head is by another account; `/resolve-conflicts check` restores `merge-ready` on an empty-remerge-diff refresh without dispatching a review and never asks an author to refresh a PR that is not about to merge; the planner runs from the repo on Windows, macOS and Linux with its own unit tests for the ordering logic; PROCESS_VERSION bumped and announced.

Filed by an agent for a contributor, who can't set labels. Suggested labels: `bug`, `P1` (a gouge that passes), `effort:high` (gouge law, safety floor), `area:verify`, `source:agent`.

**What happens.** The containment kinds' solid law excuses a hole-wall facet hit by its chord dip (`crates/sim/src/verify/swept.rs`, `chord_dip`, used from `solid_index.rs` when `hole_walls` is set):
- a facet whose three vertices all stand outside the atom's widest reach along the move is credited `rho - sqrt(rho^2 - half^2)` for each edge shorter than the atom's diameter;
- that reads every such facet as the inscribed tessellation of a round wall that the region's exact rim already judged.

A hole that really is a coarse polygon has flats that dip well inside the circle through its corners, and they get the same credit. Those flats are real material, not tessellation.

**Reproduction (from the review):**
- The fixture: #1071's `thread_mill_rim` block with an octagonal blind hole, vertices on r 5, so the flats stand at r 4.62.
- A model-sourced Thread op declared at r 4.4, with a 6 mm Tap-form thread mill at pitch 1.
- Its major circle is 4.94, off #1099's thread-wall band, so #1099's grant does not apply.
- Result: the verify gives no blocking warning, and the helix cuts about 0.32 mm into each flat. The chord dip for a 3 mm atom on the flats' 3.83 mm chords is about 0.69 mm.

The review expects a Bore on a coarse polygon hole to behave the same way. That has not been reproduced yet.

**What should happen.** The excuse should credit only tessellation of a round wall: a dip bounded by a stated mesh tolerance, as #1099 does for the thread grant (`CHORD_CREDIT` = `DEV_TOL`, 0.01 mm; the STEP importer meshes at half of it). It should not credit any chord shorter than the cutter.

**Done means:**
- an octagon (and a 16-gon) hole cut past its flats by a containment kind (Bore, and Thread off the band) convicts;
- a full-fidelity round hole (a fine 96-gon) still verifies clean for every containment kind;
- both are pinned by tests;

PR #706 grew the GUI's "Set WCS from features": pick edges, vertices, faces and cylinder walls, say which axis each one sets, and the WCS lands on the fitted frame, undoable (#701). title: Build cycle: every worktree compiles the whole dependency tree cold - share a compile cache, cut debug info, use a faster linker

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:build
labels.description: Build, CI, release, tests

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

labels.name: P5
labels.description: Agent surface and tooling keep up with what shipped

body:
Raised by the maintainer (2026-11-11): "why are we cold building complete bundles .. the tests are localized to crates".

## What happens today (measured on the dev machine)
- Every issue worker, reviewer and gate works in its own worktree with its own `target/`. A fresh one compiles the WHOLE dependency tree before the first test runs: about 15-25 minutes per review and 25-75 minutes per gate, almost all of it third-party crates (flecs' C through bindgen/cc, wgpu/egui, the B-rep kernel, the script engine ...), not our code.
- `Cargo.toml` sets `[profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 2`: every dependency is optimised in dev builds. That makes tests run faster but makes each cold build much slower.
- Nothing sets `debug`, so dev builds carry full debug info for all crates: one `target/` reaches 50-120 GB (the disk filled twice today) and every link is slow.
- Integration tests are one binary per file: `crates/app/tests` has 266 files, motion 65, sim 50. The batch gate's app step takes about 24 of its 38 minutes, much of it linking and starting 266 binaries.
- `.cargo/config.toml` holds only the `xtask` alias: no linker choice, no cache wrapper. `sccache` is not installed; `rust-lld` is.

## Wanted (this issue: the three cheap ones, measured)
1. **A shared compile cache across worktrees** (`sccache` as `RUSTC_WRAPPER`, and as the C compiler wrapper for the cc-built C code if that works on MSVC). Registry crates live at the same path for every worktree, so their compilations are cache hits; a fresh worktree should then compile only our own crates. It must be OPTIONAL: a machine without sccache builds exactly as today (enable it from `cargo xtask` / the gate wrappers when `sccache` is on PATH, or document the env var - never hard-code a wrapper in `.cargo/config.toml` that breaks a machine without it). Say how to install it and how big its cache is allowed to grow.
2. **Less debug info**: `debug = false` (or `"line-tables-only"`) for dependencies, and line tables only for our crates in dev/test - enough for backtraces and panics with file:line. Report target size and link time before/after.
3. **A faster linker** for the Windows MSVC target (`rust-lld` / `lld-link`), and the equivalent on Linux/macOS where it helps, again without breaking a machine that lacks it.
4. Re-examine `opt-level = 2` for all dependencies: keep it only for the crates whose speed the tests need (measure: batch gate time with opt-level 2 everywhere vs 1 vs a short list).

Measure and report, on the same machine, cold (empty target, warm cache where a cache applies) and warm: `cargo test -p camcraft-app --no-run`, `cargo test -p camcraft-app --test <one binary>`, `cargo xtask gate quick` on a one-file app change, and the `target/` size. No test may change behaviour; the gates stay green.

## Not in this issue (file separately if the numbers say so)
- Folding the 266 one-file app test binaries into a few binaries (one per area, files as modules). This is the biggest structural win for the gate, but it changes the gate maps in `xtask` and every "run this binary" instruction.

## Process
`.cargo/config.toml`, `xtask/` and the gate wrappers are process files: bump `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION`, and say in the PR what a fork must do.

Done means: a fresh worktree reaches its first app test at least 3x faster than today with the cache warm, `target/` is at most half today's size, the settings are optional per machine and documented, and the measured numbers are in the PR.

title: Process changes - fork maintainers please subscribe

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: P?
labels.description: Paused: never picked until the maintainer sets a real priority

body:
**Subscribe to this issue** (the "Subscribe" button on the right) if you work from a fork of CamCraft, especially with an AI agent.

Forks sync product code only at release tags (AGENTS.md "A fork syncs from upstream at each cut tag"). But the *process* - `AGENTS.md`, the agent definitions in `.claude/agents/`, the skills in `.claude/skills/` and `scripts/gate.*` - changes between releases, and a fork's agents should follow the current rules (review labels, priority labels, release steps, and so on).

**How it works:**
- `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` holds one number. Every PR that changes a process file bumps it.
- Every such PR also adds a comment **here**: the new version, what changed, and what to pull. Subscribers get one notification per change.
- A fork's agent compares its `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` with upstream's at the start of each session and, if upstream is newer, pulls just the process files (AGENTS.md "Process files sync on every session"). Product code still waits for the next release tag.

**To pull by hand:**
```
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/main -- AGENTS.md .claude/agents .claude/skills .claude/PROCESS_VERSION scripts/gate.ps1 scripts/gate.sh
git commit -m "chore(process): sync process files to upstream PROCESS_VERSION <n>"
```

This issue stays open and pinned. It's labelled `P?` so no agent ever picks it up as work.

body:
Found while working #586 (M7.3 3/6). Part of #26.

**Why #586 can't finish as a seam move:** every app stock *holder* is either a plain grid or the **carried `Body`** (`crates/sim/src/stock_sim/carry.rs`). `Body` stores the stock carried between setups as **two-sided columns**: `pub dex: Dexel` plus a per-column floor (`on_floor` / `on_mesh`). It supports the setup-change transforms that `LatticeTurn` makes exact on a lattice: XY quarter turns, Z flips and mirrors (`carry`, `deviate`'s Z-mirror via `Dexel::from_grid`, `display()`).

The app also **mutates** it as a column store:
- `simulate(&mut body.dex, ..)` in `rest/across.rs` and `rest.rs`;
- `stock_sim_carry`'s clip loop writing `dex.lower(..)`;
- `Held::Plain(Dexel)` / `Held::Carried(Body)` and `dex_mut()`.

Swapping `Dexel` for `Stock` there is a **data-model change**: carried stock on the field engine.

**Open design questions:**
1. **Representation:** the field engine holds a solid as a narrow-band SDF plus cut layers. Carrying it is a rigid transform of the field (a re-sample, or a transformed query frame) rather than a lattice permutation. Is a transformed query frame (no re-sample) exact enough for the verdicts?
2. **Floors:** a flipped part's floor is the former top. The field is a closed solid, so it has no separate floor, but "a column cut through" needs an equivalent read.
3. **Clipping** to a later setup's own stock: a field intersection (max of SDFs) replaces `lower`.
4. **Equivalence:** a heavy-lane agreement test of the carried verdicts (`setup_carry`, `rest_across_setups`, `carried_verify`) on both engines, like `stock_engine_agreement`.

**Done means:** `stock_sim_carry`, `rest`, `rest/across` and the operation priors hold carried stock as `Stock`. A field-engine carry passes the same carried-stock suites, plus an agreement lane against the column carry. #586 can then close. This is a prerequisite of #589.

Related: #26, #585 (PR #595), #586, #589, #633 (PR #636, the field block speed fix this depends on).

title: Gouge check sweeps a tap at its full diameter, so a tap on a tap-drill-size hole is refused

labels.name: area:sim
labels.description: Stock simulation and verification

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Wrong behaviour a user hits, with a workaround; fix now

body:
### What happens
The material-sim gouge check sweeps a **tap as a solid cylinder of its full (major) diameter**, the same as a drill or an end mill (`crates/app/src/stock_sim.rs` ~L240: "everything whose cut IS its cylinder - end mills, drills, taps, bores - sweeps the disc").

A tapped hole is normally modelled at the **tap-drill (minor) size**, with the thread shown cosmetically or not at all. On such a model every tap operation is refused at post time.

### Repro (found testing PR #259)
- Model: a plate with one blind Ø4 mm hole (also tried with the thread modelled).
- Drilling → Drill, tool `TAP-M6` (Ø6, 1.0 pitch), Source = the model, Detect holes → 1 hole Ø0.1575".
- Generate: OK. Post: `post refused: post blocked - gouge: program cuts below the model in 113 cell(s), worst 3.54 mm at (-0.64, -2.89, z -1.00)`.
- Remodel the hole at Ø6 (the tap's major diameter): the post passes.

So today the only way to post a tap is to model the hole at the thread's major diameter, which is not how CAD models of tapped holes look.

### Expected
A tap cuts only the thread band, between the hole's drilled wall and the tap's major diameter. The check should not call that a gouge when the tap rides an existing hole of at least roughly the tap-drill size. Possible shapes for the fix:
- For a Tap tool, sweep the tap's **minor (core) diameter**, `diameter - pitch` (ISO metric approx.; e.g. M6x1 → Ø5). The thread flanks are intended removal, not a gouge.
- And/or keep the full-diameter check only where the tap would enter solid material with no hole (a tap into an undrilled spot *is* a crash).

Pinning test: a tap on a hole modelled at the tap-drill size posts; the same tap where no hole exists is still refused.

body:
Requested by the user (2026-11-07); filed by an agent.

**Goal**: upgrade the Tool editor with a spun (revolved-profile) design editor for defining the **tool shape** and the **holder shape**, so tools can be visualized accurately in the simulation down the road.

**What it should do**
- Define a tool as a 2D half-profile (radius vs. length along the tool axis) that is spun about the axis: cutting edge / flutes, neck, shank; and the holder as its own spun profile (cone, collar, body) stacked behind the shank.
- Edit by segments (lines and arcs) or by parameters for the stock tool kinds (flat, ball, bull nose, drill, chamfer, etc.) that generate the profile; parametric edits regenerate the profile, hand edits stay a custom profile.
- **Flat preview**: a live 2D side view of the tool and holder silhouette that updates as the shape and its settings are edited, with key dimensions (diameter, flute length, shank, stickout/gauge length, holder diameter and length) drawn on it.
- Validation at the door: a profile must be closed to the axis, monotonic where it must be, with positive radii and finite numbers; an invalid profile is refused by name, never saved.

**Why**: the simulation and the collision/reach checks (#84 drill reach, holder clearance; verify shank/holder laws) currently read the tool as a few cylinders (flute, shank, holder). A spun profile gives them the true silhouette - the field sweep, holder clearance and future 3D tool rendering can all read the same shape.

**Done means**
- Tool and holder shapes stored as spun profiles in the tool library (with a migration from today's diameter/length fields; project-file version bump if the format changes).
- The Tool editor shows the flat preview, updating live; edits go through undoable commands (AGENTS.md "Everything Is a Command").
- Existing tools load with a profile equal to their current cylinders, so behaviour is unchanged until a shape is edited.
- Tests: profile validation (refusals by name), migration round-trip, preview snapshot.

**Out of scope (follow-ups)**: 3D tool rendering in the viewport and feeding the profile into the stock simulation and collision laws - this issue lays the data and the editor they will read.
